title: Centroid of a Tree
directAnswer: A centroid of a tree is a node whose removal leaves every remaining component with at most n/2 nodes. Compute subtree sizes with one DFS, then a node is a centroid iff its largest 'piece' — the bigger of (its heaviest child subtree) and (n minus its own subtree, the part above it) — is ≤ ⌊n/2⌋. A tree has one centroid, or two adjacent centroids when n is even. Finding it is O(n).

remember.pattern: Subtree-size DFS, then test max(child subtrees, rest-of-tree) ≤ n/2
remember.formula:
size[node] = 1 + Σ size[child]
for each node:
    biggest = max over children of size[child]
    biggest = max(biggest, n - size[node])   # the part above node
    if biggest <= n // 2: node is a centroid
rules: The 'piece above' a node has size **n − size[node]** — do not forget it; it is the most-missed component.
A node is a centroid iff its **largest component after removal ≤ ⌊n/2⌋**.
Every tree has **1 or 2** centroids; **2** (adjacent) happen exactly when n is even and the tree is balanced across one edge.
Centroid sizes are computed from any root — rooting does not change the answer, only how you phrase 'above'.
Walking from any start toward the heaviest neighbor whose subtree > n/2 reaches a centroid in O(n).
whenToUse: Balancing a tree for divide-and-conquer (centroid decomposition)
Bounding recursion depth: rooting at the centroid limits component size to n/2
Problems over all paths in a tree solved by splitting at a balanced node
Minimizing the maximum subtree size after removing one node
antiSignals: You need the node minimizing total distance to all others → that is also the centroid, but state it as the 1-median; same node, different framing
You need the center (minimizing eccentricity / tree radius) → that is a different node found by peeling leaves (BFS)
Weighted 'balance' by edge length, not node count → adapt the size definition accordingly
Graph has cycles → 'centroid' is undefined; this relies on the tree structure
remember.takeaway: The centroid is the tree's balance point: remove it and no leftover piece exceeds half the tree. One subtree-size DFS plus remembering the 'piece above' (n − size) finds it in O(n), and it is the anchor that makes centroid decomposition's O(n log n) divide-and-conquer work.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you compute subtree sizes correctly and — the real test — remember that removing a node also creates the component ABOVE it of size n − size[node], not just the child subtrees.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Only checking child subtree sizes and ignoring the n − size[node] part above the node, or confusing the centroid (balances component sizes) with the center (minimizes height).
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Define the centroid precisely, derive the ≤ n/2 test from the size DFS, explain the 1-or-2 centroid fact, and note the O(n) 'walk toward the heavy child' method plus its role in centroid decomposition.

problemStatement:
Given a tree with `n` nodes, find a ***centroid***: a node such that, if it is removed, every connected component that remains has at most `⌊n/2⌋` nodes.

Return any centroid (there may be two adjacent ones). Your solution should run in ***O(n)***.
constraints: The graph is a tree: connected, n − 1 edges, no cycles
Nodes are 0-indexed; the tree is given as an edge list
A tree always has at least one centroid; even-n balanced trees have two adjacent centroids
understanding: We want the most 'balanced' node — the one whose removal does not leave any oversized chunk. Removing a node splits the tree into pieces: one per child subtree, plus the whole rest of the tree hanging above the node. The centroid is the node whose biggest such piece is as small as possible, and that minimum is guaranteed to be ≤ n/2. The single non-obvious part is accounting for the piece above the node, whose size is n minus the node's own subtree.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Centroid or center — which do you mean?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Centroid: removing it balances component sizes (≤ n/2 each). The center minimizes tree height/eccentricity and is found by peeling leaves. They can differ; I will solve the centroid.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can there be more than one centroid?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: One or two. Two occur (and are always adjacent) exactly when n is even and an edge splits the tree into two equal n/2 halves.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is balance by node count or something weighted?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Node count here. If pieces were weighted, I would replace 'size' with the summed weight and keep the same logic.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How deep can the tree be?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to n in a chain, so the size DFS should be iterative (explicit stack) to avoid a recursion-stack overflow at 2×10⁵ nodes.

examples.input: star: center 0 connected to 1,2,3,4 (n=5); find centroid
examples.explanation: Removing 0 leaves four singletons (size 1 each ≤ 2). Removing any leaf leaves a component of size 4 > 2. So 0 is the unique centroid.
n is even. Removing 1 gives pieces {0} and {2,3}: sizes 1 and 2 ≤ 2. Removing 2 gives {0,1} and {3}: 2 and 1. Both 1 and 2 are centroids — adjacent, as the even-n rule predicts.
Removing it leaves nothing; the trivial centroid is the node itself.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Remove Each Node, Measure the Pieces
approaches.whenToMention: Say this first: it defines a centroid operationally and makes the n − size insight visible before optimizing.
hints: For each candidate node, imagine deleting it and run a BFS/DFS over the rest to measure every resulting component.
If the largest component is ≤ n/2, the candidate is a centroid.
Each test is an O(n) traversal and there are n candidates → O(n²). Correct, but it screams 'precompute the sizes once'.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Removing a node and measuring components is an O(n) traversal; repeating for all n candidates gives O(n²). Fine for small n, too slow at 2×10⁵.
approaches.explanation:
The definition is constructive, so the brute force just follows it.

**For each candidate.** Pretend to delete the node, then traverse the remaining forest to find the size of each connected component.

**Test the balance.** If the maximum component size is at most `⌊n/2⌋`, the candidate qualifies as a centroid; otherwise move on.

**Why it is correct.** It literally checks the centroid condition for every node, so it cannot be fooled.

**Why it is slow.** Each candidate costs an O(n) traversal, and there are n of them — O(n²). The redundancy is that every traversal recomputes the same subtree sizes. Compute those sizes *once* with a single DFS and each candidate's pieces can be read off in O(1): the child subtree sizes are stored, and the piece above is `n − size[node]`.
approaches.insight: Doing the deletion explicitly reveals the components you must measure — including the one above the node. The optimization is purely that those component sizes are all derivable from a single subtree-size DFS, so the n repeated traversals collapse into one.

dryRun.intro: Delete a node, measure remaining components, check max ≤ 2.

java.explanation: Measure the biggest leftover piece after deleting this candidate.
Re-traverses the whole tree per candidate — the O(n²) cost.

python.explanation: Scan all unvisited starts to find every component — repeated for each candidate.

pitfalls: Forgetting that deleting an internal node creates a component above it as well as below.
Recomputing component sizes for every candidate — the redundancy the size DFS removes.
Using n/2 with the wrong rounding — use ⌊n/2⌋ consistently.

approaches.name: Subtree-Size DFS — Single Pass (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. 'One DFS for subtree sizes, then each node's largest piece is max(heaviest child, n − size[node]).'
hints: Root the tree anywhere and compute size[node] = 1 + sum of children's sizes with one DFS.
When you remove a node, the pieces are its child subtrees (sizes already known) plus the part above it, whose size is n − size[node].
A node is a centroid iff the maximum of those pieces is ≤ n/2. Check every node in a second linear scan (or fold it into the DFS).
approaches.complexityReasoning: One DFS computes all subtree sizes in O(n). A second O(n) scan evaluates each node's largest piece in O(deg) using stored sizes, summing to O(n). Total O(n) time, O(n) space for sizes and the stack.
approaches.explanation:
Compute the structure once, then read off the answer.

**Step 1 — subtree sizes.** Root the tree at any node (say 0) and compute `size[node] = 1 + Σ size[child]` with a single post-order DFS. `size[node]` counts the node and everything below it in this rooting.

**Step 2 — the pieces created by removal.** Deleting `node` disconnects the tree into:
- one component per child, of size `size[child]`, and
- the component *above* `node` — everything not in `node`'s subtree — of size `n − size[node]`.

The largest piece for `node` is therefore `max( max over children size[child], n − size[node] )`. The second term is the one candidates forget; it is exactly the rest of the tree hanging above the node through its parent.

**Step 3 — the centroid test.** `node` is a centroid iff that largest piece is `≤ ⌊n/2⌋`. Scan all nodes and return any that pass. Because the sizes are precomputed, each node's check is O(deg), so the whole scan is O(n).

**Why a centroid always exists, and why ≤ n/2.** Start anywhere and repeatedly move to the neighbor whose component (after cutting the edge you came from) exceeds n/2. Each move strictly decreases the size of the heaviest piece, so the walk terminates — at a node where no piece exceeds n/2, the centroid. That same walk is an alternative O(n) algorithm: from the root, keep stepping into the child whose subtree size > n/2 until none qualifies.

**Why one or two centroids.** If some node has a child subtree of exactly n/2 (only possible when n is even), then both that node and that child satisfy the ≤ n/2 test, and they are adjacent. Otherwise the centroid is unique. There can never be three, because a third would force a piece larger than n/2 somewhere.

**Centroid vs center.** The centroid balances *sizes* (this problem). The *center* minimizes *height* (tree radius) and is found by repeatedly removing all current leaves until one or two nodes remain. They sometimes coincide but are different in general — naming the right one is part of the interview.
approaches.insight: Everything hinges on a single accounting identity: removing a node leaves child subtrees you already measured plus a top piece of size n − size[node]. Once you internalize that the 'rest above' is just n minus the subtree, the centroid test is a one-line max comparison, and the whole problem is one DFS.

edgeCases.behavior: Single node is its own centroid; handled before the DFS.
Both nodes are centroids: removing either leaves one node (size 1 ≤ 1). Two adjacent centroids — the even-n case.

edgeCases.input: perfectly balanced even tree across one edge
edgeCases.behavior: Two adjacent centroids, each with a child subtree of exactly n/2; the scan returns the first one found.

pitfalls: Checking only child subtrees and ignoring the n − size[node] piece above the node.
Confusing the centroid (balances sizes) with the center (minimizes height).
Recursive size DFS on a chain of 2×10⁵ nodes — stack overflow; use an explicit stack.
Rounding n/2 inconsistently — use integer ⌊n/2⌋ throughout.

commonMistakes: Ignoring the component above the node (size n − size[node]) and only checking child subtrees.
Confusing the centroid with the center of the tree.
Overflowing the stack with a recursive size DFS on a long chain.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Forgetting the piece above the node
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Removing an internal node creates the child-subtree pieces AND the whole rest of the tree above it. That upper piece has size n − size[node]; skip it and almost every node looks like a centroid.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Centroid vs center confusion
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The center minimizes tree height (found by peeling leaves) while the centroid balances component sizes. They can be different nodes; solving the wrong one fails the test even with correct code.
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
# Centroid: balance sizes
largest = max(n - size[node], max((size[c] for c in children), default=0))
if largest <= n // 2:
    return node

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Recursive size DFS overflow
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A chain of 2×10⁵ nodes recurses 2×10⁵ deep, overflowing the default call stack in both Java and Python. Compute subtree sizes with an explicit stack and a reverse-order pass.

followupVariations.title: Centroid Decomposition
followupVariations.hint: Recursively make the centroid the root of its component; depth is O(log n), enabling divide-and-conquer over all paths.

followupVariations.title: Minimum Height Trees
followupVariations.hint: Finds the tree CENTER (1 or 2 nodes) by peeling leaves — contrast with the centroid here.

followupVariations.title: Sum of Distances in Tree
followupVariations.hint: Re-rooting DP; the node minimizing total distance is the centroid (1-median) view of balance.

followupVariations.title: Heavy-Light Decomposition
followupVariations.hint: Another size-driven decomposition; the heavy-child idea mirrors the largest-subtree reasoning used here.

patternNote: Centroid of a tree: compute subtree sizes with one DFS, then a node is a centroid iff its largest piece after removal — max(heaviest child subtree, n − size[node]) — is ≤ ⌊n/2⌋. There are one or two (adjacent) centroids, found in O(n). It is the balance point that anchors centroid decomposition.
